This is Disney's Moana Call of the Ocean. Long ago on an island surrounded by seas, a girl named Moana, the daughter of Chief Tui, was born. Moana loved listening to ancient stories told by her grandma Tala about the mischievous demigod Maui and Teiti, the mother island. From a young age, Moana felt the ocean calling her. One day it brought her a gift. The spiral heart of Teiti. "You must learn where you're meant to be," Chief Tui would say. Now 16 years old, Moana's heart is full of adventure, and she longs to know what is beyond the reef surrounding her house. But her father Tui is not happy with his daughter's dream. The ocean is dangerous and Moana is needed by her people. You are the future of our people, Moana. Grandma Tala takes Moana to an ancient cave and shares a secret with her. Long ago, their people were voyagers until Maui stole the heart of Teiti and darkness fell on the islands. Grandma Tala believes Moana is chosen to restore life to their island. She must find Teiti and give her back the heart. Moana takes a boat from the cave and sets sail. The ocean chose you, Grandma Tala. When Moana finds Maui, she says, "I am Moana of Monteneui. You will board my boat, sail across the sea, and restore the heart of Teiti." Maui refuses to go with her, but Moana does not give up, and Maui finally agrees to help her. As they journey across the sea, Maui teaches Moana the ancient art of wayfying. It's not just sails and knots. It's seeing where you're going in your mind, Maui. When things don't go as planned, Maui leaves Moana alone in her boat. Moana wants to give up. But grandma appears and speaks to her. Moana listens and knows what she must do. She set off alone for Teiti, ready to save her people. What does the voice inside say? Grandma Tala. Maui has done some thinking, too. He returns as a giant hawk to help his friend. Together they battle Tea and restore Teiti's heart. I've got your back, chosen one. Go save the world. Maui, when Moana returns to her village, she knows who she is meant to be. She is Moana of Matanoui, leader, wayfinder, friend. Maui, you could come with us. You know, my people are going to need a master wayfinder. They already have one. Maui.

The morning sun rose high over Monteneui as Moana headed through the village. "Good morning," Moana said, approaching two women with baskets of food. How are things? Hi, Moana. It's a fine day, but we're low on sugar cane and we won't have enough for what we're making. I can help. Moana volunteered. I'll gather some more for you. Can we come too? A girl named Fatua asked Moana. We love exploring. Yes, but we all have to stick together. The island is big and I don't want anyone to get lost. But if something does happen, just stay where you are and wait for me to come find you. Moana said, "We promise." The children said they were so excited to spend the day with Moana. Moana and the children set off toward the forest. I love sugar cane. A girl named Msina said. Moana and the children talked about how many things they use sugar cane for. I like to just eat it by itself. A boy named Toa said. The forest was full of giant trees, colorful plants, and rocks and boulders of all sizes. Without any clear paths to walk along, it was obvious why Moana had told them to stick together. Moana looked for visual signs to help her find her way. "See, that rock over there looks a little like Pua," Moana said. The kids loved Pua and could picture him as if he were right there. Moana pulled aside some thick green vines revealing a large grove of coconut trees. Can we stop for a snack? La asked. That's just what I was thinking. Moana replied. Lame and Toas scrambled up a tree. They picked the ripest fruits, then tossed them down. After they broke open the coconuts against a rock, they devoured the white meat and drank the sweet water inside. It was a refreshing break. "Do we have time for a game?" Fatua asked. Since they'd reached the coconut grove sooner than Moana had expected, she figured a quick game wouldn't hurt. "How about a round of hide and seek?" she asked. "Yes," the children exclaimed. They scattered in every direction. "But stay close by," Moana called after them. She shut her eyes and began to count. While he was looking for a place to hide, Toa saw a colorful bird he'd never seen before. He began to follow the bird. "Times up!" Moana yelled. She opened her eyes and began to look for the children. In a matter of minutes, Moana had found Fatoua, Laame, and Msina. That meant only Toa was left. But no matter where she looked, Moana couldn't find him. "Good job, Toa. You found the best hiding spot. You can come out now," Moana said. When he didn't appear, Moana was worried he was lost. Meanwhile, Toa had followed the colorful bird all the way back to its nest. He turned around to show his friends, but realized he was all alone. He started to worry, but he remembered what Moana had said earlier, and he sat down and waited for her to find him. Moana and the other children went back through the vines toward the pu-shaped rock. It was there that Moana noticed some bright blue feathers. Maybe he went up this way, she said. They picked up the feathers and continued walking. Not far away, they came upon another clearing, and there was someone familiar sitting on a rock. "Toa!" Fatua cried as Moana hugged him. They were relieved to see he was safe and sound. "I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't mean to go so far off. I was following that bird and it ended up here." He pointed to a nest in a tree hollow. Moana looked up to see a bird with several baby chicks. Toa had stumbled upon a mother bird as she was returning to her family. "Well, it looks like everyone is back together again," Moana said, smiling. "Look over there," directed Fatua. That's the tallest grass I've ever seen," added Masina. Moana followed the girls and couldn't believe her eyes. Thanks to their unexpected detour, they had found a shortcut to the sugar cane field. "This is exactly what we're looking for," Moana cheered. She broke off pieces of the sugar cane stalks and passed them to the children who arranged them in piles. After gathering as much as their arms could carry, it was time to head home. "Before we go," Moana said, "Let's create a sign to mark this new shortcut." They carved an outline of the bird into the ground with sticks. Finally, they stuck the blue feathers they'd collected in the ground next to their new landmark. It was a perfect way to end their afternoon. Soon, Moana and the children arrived back in the village. Moana gave the basket of sugar cane to the women who were delighted to see the bright, juicy stalks. "Thank you, Moana," one woman exclaimed. These are wonderful. It was our pleasure, Moana replied. As they said goodbye, Moana gave each child a hungi, pressing her nose against theirs. "When I grow up, I want to be like you," Toa said. Moana was touched. As Grandma Tala says, you can be whatever your heart tells you. Moana smiled all the way home. Her heart felt as full as the baskets of sugar cane.

The morning sun rose high over Monteneui as Moana headed through the village. "Good morning," Moana said, approaching two women with baskets of food. How are things? Hi, Moana. It's a fine day, but we're low on sugar cane and we won't have enough for what we're making. I can help. Moana volunteered. I'll gather some more for you. Can we come too? A girl named Fatua asked Moana. We love exploring. Yes, but we all have to stick together. The island is big and I don't want anyone to get lost. But if something does happen, just stay where you are and wait for me to come find you. Moana said, "We promise." The children said they were so excited to spend the day with Moana. Moana and the children set off toward the forest. I love sugar cane. A girl named Msina said. Moana and the children talked about how many things they use sugar cane for. I like to just eat it by itself. A boy named Toa said. The forest was full of giant trees, colorful plants, and rocks and boulders of all sizes. Without any clear paths to walk along, it was obvious why Moana had told them to stick together. Moana looked for visual signs to help her find her way. "See, that rock over there looks a little like Pua," Moana said. The kids loved Pua and could picture him as if he were right there. Moana pulled aside some thick green vines revealing a large grove of coconut trees. Can we stop for a snack? La asked. That's just what I was thinking. Moana replied. Lame and Toas scrambled up a tree. They picked the ripest fruits, then tossed them down. After they broke open the coconuts against a rock, they devoured the white meat and drank the sweet water inside. It was a refreshing break. "Do we have time for a game?" Fatua asked. Since they'd reached the coconut grove sooner than Moana had expected, she figured a quick game wouldn't hurt. "How about a round of hide and seek?" she asked. "Yes," the children exclaimed. They scattered in every direction. "But stay close by," Moana called after them. She shut her eyes and began to count. While he was looking for a place to hide, Toa saw a colorful bird he'd never seen before. He began to follow the bird. "Times up!" Moana yelled. She opened her eyes and began to look for the children. In a matter of minutes, Moana had found Fatoua, Laame, and Msina. That meant only Toa was left. But no matter where she looked, Moana couldn't find him. "Good job, Toa. You found the best hiding spot. You can come out now," Moana said. When he didn't appear, Moana was worried he was lost. Meanwhile, Toa had followed the colorful bird all the way back to its nest. He turned around to show his friends, but realized he was all alone. He started to worry, but he remembered what Moana had said earlier, and he sat down and waited for her to find him. Moana and the other children went back through the vines toward the pu-shaped rock. It was there that Moana noticed some bright blue feathers. Maybe he went up this way, she said. They picked up the feathers and continued walking. Not far away, they came upon another clearing, and there was someone familiar sitting on a rock. "Toa!" Fatua cried as Moana hugged him. They were relieved to see he was safe and sound. "I'm sorry," he said. "I didn't mean to go so far off. I was following that bird and it ended up here." He pointed to a nest in a tree hollow. Moana looked up to see a bird with several baby chicks. Toa had stumbled upon a mother bird as she was returning to her family. "Well, it looks like everyone is back together again," Moana said, smiling. "Look over there," directed Fatua. That's the tallest grass I've ever seen," added Masina. Moana followed the girls and couldn't believe her eyes. Thanks to their unexpected detour, they had found a shortcut to the sugar cane field. "This is exactly what we're looking for," Moana cheered. She broke off pieces of the sugar cane stalks and passed them to the children who arranged them in piles. After gathering as much as their arms could carry, it was time to head home. "Before we go," Moana said, "Let's create a sign to mark this new shortcut." They carved an outline of the bird into the ground with sticks. Finally, they stuck the blue feathers they'd collected in the ground next to their new landmark. It was a perfect way to end their afternoon. Soon, Moana and the children arrived back in the village. Moana gave the basket of sugar cane to the women who were delighted to see the bright, juicy stalks. "Thank you, Moana," one woman exclaimed. These are wonderful. It was our pleasure, Moana replied. As they said goodbye, Moana gave each child a hungi, pressing her nose against theirs. "When I grow up, I want to be like you," Toa said. Moana was touched. As Grandma Tala says, you can be whatever your heart tells you. Moana smiled all the way home. Her heart felt as full as the baskets of sugar cane.
